finding.headline: About 15% of your pay goes to tax now; retirement tax looks lower.
details: Now you pay about $7,970 in tax on $52,000 of pay, which is 15%. In retirement, the part-time work and Social Security would carry about 11% tax on the part-time pay.
All of your savings sit in taxable and cash accounts, so you draw on those first. Pre-tax and Roth accounts come later if you open them.
This is a rough guide, not tax advice. Check the details with a tax professional before you act.

finding.headline: Plan for your money to last to age 92.
details: You are 56 and plan to retire at 59, so the money must cover about 33 years of retirement.
At age 92, there is about a 24% chance you are still alive. There is a 31% chance someone in the household reaches 90.

finding.headline: You have no children, college, or pet costs, so your main costs are basics and a kitchen remodel.
details: Once you retire, the basics cost about $34,600 a year, or $2,883 a month. Health coverage before Medicare at 65 is about $10,000 a year.
You plan a $45,000 kitchen remodel in 2034. Your car loan is $7,100, with payments of $1,800 a year.
Long-term nursing home care, if needed, is about $129,575 a year for about 3 years. Plan for that cost separately.

finding.headline: You retire at 59, before Medicare starts at 65, so plan for 6 years of health coverage.
details: Medicare generally starts when you turn 65. Your sign-up window runs 7 months, from 3 months before to 3 months after the month you turn 65. Missing it can mean a monthly late penalty for as long as you have Part B.

At 60 to 63, the 401(k) catch-up limit rises to $11,750 for 2027, instead of $8,500 at 50 and older. Your retirement at 59 falls just before this window, so use the $8,500 catch-up limit until you reach 60.
The 401(k) limit rises to $25,500 for 2027, and the IRA limit stays at $7,500.

assumptions: All figures are in today's dollars: what money buys now, not the larger sums prices will reach.

Savings grow on average 5.0% a year above inflation in stocks and 1.8% in bonds, with good and bad years. The plan tests many possible market paths. These are planning figures, not a forecast. They are fixed, so every plan is tested on the same markets; to see a bad stretch, try a What If such as markets fall 30%.
Your spending now is about $870 a year more than your take-home pay, so until you retire the plan takes that from your savings each year. If that is wrong, change your spending now or your pay.
Pay stays at today's level until you retire, with no raises. This is fixed: raises are not certain, so the plan does not count on them. If your pay changes, change it in your answers.
Social Security uses the figure you gave, read as the benefit at 67. Your answers show $21,900 a year from 67. This plan starts it at 62, which pays about $15,300 a year.
If you retire before Medicare starts at 65, health cover costs about $10,000 a person a year until then (an assumption). Other health costs follow CMS figures by age.

Tax uses the 2027 federal brackets, the standard deduction and your state's rates. While you work, 401(k) saving comes off taxable pay. In retirement the plan counts 85% of Social Security as taxable, the most the law allows, so the tax may be a little high.
The plan runs to age 92. There is about a 1 in 4 chance that you will live that long (US life table, SOA 2024). People with more money tend to live longer than that table says.
